B3:
**B3 — Returns correct shortened string (algorithm).**

Judge B3 on what the method, taken exactly as written, would actually return for a typical valid username: read the loop bounds, the indices, and the location the response found for the hyphen from the rest of the method, and ask whether the end-to-end result is the correct shortened string. Deduct whenever that end-to-end result is wrong — e.g., a loop bounded by a constant (`i < 10`) or an index/hyphen search that is off, so the final returned string is wrong, even if the substring/concatenation logic is otherwise textbook; likewise deduct for failing to return the string, incorrectly building it (early return, bad initialization), modifying `username`, or printing instead of (or in addition to) returning. No_deduct only when the string that would actually come back is the correct one.

Within that end-to-end judgment, two classes of flaw are excused rather than treated as algorithmic defects. First, misuse of the String API itself: a wrong method name, wrong argument order, or wrong number of arguments (e.g., `username.substring(i, 0)` or `username.subString(0, i)`), and comparing one-character substrings with `==` instead of `.equals`, all count as the excused "call any String method incorrectly" case — if the intended selection, concatenation, and return of the right pieces of the string is clear and correct, give the point. Second, compilation-level slips unrelated to the algorithm — an undeclared variable, a missing brace, returning a value whose type is slightly off — are no_deduct when the intended construction and return of the correct string is unambiguous.

So: deduct only for algorithmic defects in building and returning the shortened string, assessed on the code as written end to end; no_deduct for malformed String calls, `==` string comparison, and non-algorithmic syntax/compilation slips when the intended correct string is unambiguous.
